extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political theory and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria for designing or judging constitutions, especially rules about separation of powers, representation, checks and balances, and protections against faction and usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of legislative and executive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The law-making (legislative) and law-executing (executive) powers ought to be kept distinctly flowing in distinct channels so that they may never meet in one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as central to 'the safety of the state.' The text argues that whenever those powers are united (in one person or body), injustice results and the people are left without remedy. Historical examples (Rome, Sparta, Athens, France, Spain, Venice) are given to show the ruin that follows when the powers are united.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence and appointment by the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive ought to be appointed by the people in the formation of their constitution as much as the legislative; the executive represents the majesty, persons, wills, and power of the people in administration and dispensing of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the view that the executive is 'derived' from the legislature; both legislative and executive are derived from the people. Executive must be as distinct and independent of the legislative as the legislative is of it to prevent the executive becoming a mere tool of the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive the executive from the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: If the executive is appointed by, or derived from, the legislative, it is in effect one power and in the same hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment of the executive by the legislature makes the executive a weathercock subject to the leading members of the house; military, judicial, and administrative powers will bow to legislative influence. Such nominal separation is insecure and facilitates intrigue and artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping powers in 'indifferent hands' to preserve accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the power of making laws, executing them, and administering justice into different, indifferent hands to preserve equity, equality, and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When powers are kept asunder the people have governors liable to account to the supreme councils; when united, arbitrary power creeps in. Examples include historical transitions where concentration produced tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engrossing public transactions and interests in the hands of a few
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent reducing public transactions and interests into the disposition and power of a few particular persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public business is carried by private design and surprise (premeditated resolutions of crafty projectors in private juntos), decisions cease to be by fair debate and instead serve private ends. This fosters corruption, secrecy, and loss of popular benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide legal, constitutional, habitual modes for resolving precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a legal, constitutional, and habitual mode of always determining who shall be foremost to prevent perpetual struggles for the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without settled rules determining precedence, simple governments will be perpetually distracted by contests for supremacy, leading to instability and factionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances (including a 'triple balance') to guard against faction
rubrics_metrics.description: A triple balance of powers (the one, the few, and the many) or equivalent system of countervailing institutions affords a remedy against faction and domination by any one estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factions arise from the one, the few, or the many; equalization among distinct centers of authority is proposed as a never-failing remedy. Historical evidence of faction-driven ruin (Rome, Carthage, Athens) supports this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the people across multiple bodies and acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The people should be represented by every power and body in the state and in every act they do (e.g., legislature, executive, judges, juries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation in courts (judges and juries) and in assemblies provides accountability and avenues of redress; officers should be liable to give account to representative bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the executive a mere tool of the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not vest appointment or disposal of executive commissions in legislative masters so that executive, military, and judicial powers become instruments of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legislative bodies control appointments, commissions, military discipline, and judicial compliance, those branches become prostituted to corrupt influence and elections become compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation must be substantive, not merely nominal
rubrics_metrics.description: A separation of powers that exists only in name (e.g., executive nominally appointed but effectively controlled by legislature) is not a real safeguard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses that historical 'mixed' forms sometimes only separated powers in appearance; true security requires functional separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'reason of state' as a blanket justification for tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not permit leaders to allege 'reason of state' as a pretext to justify all species of tyranny and oppression over minorities or even over their own party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that majorities or leaders may repeatedly invoke 'reason of state' to excuse encroachments, ultimately enabling arbitrary rule; constitutions should limit such executive or majority prerogatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent private cabals and premeditated resolutions from supplanting public debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional design should block mechanisms by which small private groups (juntos) decide public affairs in secrecy, supplanting open deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public business is planned in private cabinets, decisions reflect private ends not public good; this leads to deception of the people and erosion of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical precedent as a diagnostic for institutional failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess institutional arrangements against historical examples showing how concentration or misallocation of powers produced injustice, civil war, or loss of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly invokes examples (the thirty tyrants of Athens, triumvirates of Rome, Venice, Spain, France, etc.) to demonstrate patterns of failure and to justify the proposed principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against faction-driven cycles of replacement and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate that factions and juntas who seize power tend to fight among themselves, causing civil strife and eventual rise of a single tyrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (successive juntas in Athens, triumvirates in Rome, baronial confederacies in England) show that temporary concentrations among a few produce cycles of emulation, betrayal, civil war, and ultimately singular domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure avenues of appeal and remedy against abuse of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Design institutions so that the people have remedies against those who wield supreme power (i.e., appeals, accountable councils, judicial review mechanisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lawmakers are also constant administrators, the people are left without remedy; separation and representative oversight are advocated as means to preserve redress and justice.
